summary: Defines media types for the W3C Speech Interface Framework languages: VoiceXML, SSML, SRGS, CCXML, and PLS. These were designed by the W3C Voice Browser Working Group, and registering their media types lets software recognize and handle them. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Computers that talk and listen use special file types. This memo gives each file type an official name tag.

questions: how do i register voice interface media types
subtitle: Official media types for W3C voice and speech languages

tldr.problem: Voice application builders need standard ways to identify and process five W3C Speech Interface Framework languages (VoiceXML, SSML, SRGS, CCXML, and PLS).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4267 registers six MIME media types for these languages, with both XML (+xml) and ABNF variants, allowing software to recognize files by their content type.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now handle voice interface files correctly and interoperably by looking up the registered media types.

today: RFC 4267 is an Informational RFC that registers MIME media types for W3C voice interface languages. These registrations enable web servers and applications to correctly identify and process voice interface files.

sections.title: Voice Interface Framework Overview
sections.content: The W3C Speech Interface Framework is a collection of five specifications designed for building voice-based applications. VoiceXML is an XML language for creating audio dialogs with synthesized speech, voice recognition, and DTMF key input. SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) lets developers control speech synthesis details like pronunciation, volume, pitch, and rate. SRGS (Speech Recognition Grammar Specification) defines the words and patterns a speech recognizer should listen for, with both ABNF and XML syntax forms. CCXML (Call Control XML) provides telephony call control for dialog systems. PLS (Pronunciation Lexicon Specification) specifies pronunciation for speech engines.
sections.eli5: These are five different languages for building voice apps. Each one does a different job, like playing voice messages or understanding what someone said.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration
sections.content: RFC 4267 registers six MIME media types. Five languages get XML-based types: application/voicexml+xml, application/ssml+xml, application/srgs+xml, application/ccxml+xml, and application/pls+xml. The SRGS grammar format also has a non-XML ABNF form registered as application/srgs. All types are in the application category. The only optional parameter across all types is charset, which follows the same rules as application/xml.
sections.eli5: The RFC says 'When you get a file with this label, it is a VoiceXML file' (or SSML, or one of the others). Now programs know what they are receiving.

sections.title: Format Details and File Extensions
sections.content: The XML-based media types inherit encoding and fragment identifier rules from RFC 3023. VoiceXML files use the .vxml extension, SSML uses .ssml, SRGS XML grammar uses .grxml, CCXML uses .ccxml, and PLS uses .pls. The ABNF form of SRGS uses the .gram extension and requires a self-identifying header: the file must start with a '#' symbol followed by 'ABNF' and a version number (like '1.0' for this specification). Both XML and ABNF forms must support UTF-8 and UTF-16 encodings.
sections.eli5: Each type has a file extension so humans and programs can see what kind of file it is at a glance, like '.vxml' for voice files.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: Since these languages can reference external URIs, the security considerations from RFC 3986 apply. For example, a VoiceXML file might tell a phone to fetch a voice prompt from a URL, which requires careful validation. All five specifications have extensibility features that might carry unexpected content. However, RFC 4267 notes that if a processor strictly follows only the normative semantics specified in the W3C documents, any extension content will be ignored. Security issues only arise if the processor chooses to recognize and process non-normative extensions, which then falls outside this registration document's scope.
sections.eli5: Files can point to other files on the internet, so be careful about where the files come from, like checking that a URL is trustworthy before using it.

sections.title: Interoperability and Applications
sections.content: There are no known interoperability issues with these media type registrations. Various W3C Speech Interface Framework implementations use these media types to exchange voice interface files across systems. The W3C Voice Browser Working Group maintains control over the specifications themselves. Organizations implementing voice systems can register these media types with their web servers and content management systems, ensuring that voice interface files are served with the correct MIME type headers. This enables client applications to automatically recognize and process voice files correctly.
sections.eli5: Many companies have built tools that understand these languages. Once they know the file type from the MIME label, they can handle it correctly.

references.text: Murata, M., St. Laurent, S., and D. Kohn, "XML Media Types", RFC 3023, January 2001.
Berners-Lee, T., Fielding, R., and L. Masinter, "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax", STD 66, RFC 3986, January 2005.
